chunks.text: Step through it, or hit Auto Play to watch the full round trip happen on its own. This is the payoff of the whole Computer Functions section so far: a web request touches nearly everything you've learned — a CPU running instructions, RAM and cache holding data close by, disk storing it permanently, and now a network carrying it between machines entirely. None of these ideas exist in isolation; every real system leans on all of them at once.

chunks.title: Packets & IP Addresses
chunks.text: When you send something over a network — a message, a photo, a request for a web page — it doesn't travel as one single blob. It gets sliced into small pieces called packets, each one sent off on its own, and put back together in the right order once every piece has arrived.

chunks.title: Packets & IP Addresses
chunks.heading: Why not just send it as one piece?
chunks.text: Picture mailing a long letter by tearing it into a stack of numbered postcards and dropping them in the mail separately, instead of one big envelope. That sounds strange for a letter — but for data, it's genuinely useful: If one small packet gets lost or damaged along the way, only that piece needs to be resent — not the entire file. Many different conversations can share the same wires fairly, packet by packet, instead of one huge transfer hogging the connection the whole time. Different packets from the same message can even take slightly different paths and still all arrive — they just get sorted back into order using their sequence number once they land.

chunks.title: Packets & IP Addresses
chunks.heading: Every packet needs an address: the IP address
chunks.text: For a packet to find its way, every device on a network needs a unique address — an IP address (like 192.168.1.5 on a home network, or a public one for a server out on the internet). It works exactly like a street address: it's how a packet knows where it's headed, and it's how the reply knows where to come back to.

chunks.title: Packets & IP Addresses
chunks.heading: Visual model: split a message, then reassemble it
chunks.text: Type a short message, send it, and watch it split into packets that arrive out of order — then reassemble them using their sequence numbers. This is exactly the same principle you saw with SQLite and Postgres reading fixed-size pages from disk instead of the whole file at once — breaking big things into small, individually-addressable pieces shows up everywhere in computing, not just networks.

chunks.title: Routers: The Path Data Takes
chunks.text: A packet almost never travels straight from your device to its destination in one jump. It passes through a chain of devices called routers, each one looking at the packet's address and forwarding it one step closer to where it's going.

chunks.title: Routers: The Path Data Takes
chunks.heading: Like a postal sorting system
chunks.text: Your letter doesn't go directly from your mailbox to the recipient's — it passes through a local sorting office, maybe a regional hub, then a hub closer to the destination, then finally local delivery. Routers do the same job for data: your home router hands the packet to your internet provider's router, which hands it toward the destination's network, which hands it to the right server — often five, ten, or more hops in total.

chunks.title: Routers: The Path Data Takes
chunks.heading: Each router only needs to know "which way is closer"
chunks.text: No single router needs to know the entire path in advance. It just needs to know, for a given address, which direction gets a packet closer to home — the same way a sorting clerk doesn't need to know your exact street, just which regional hub to send it toward next. Each hop narrows things down a little more, until the packet lands at the right doorstep.

chunks.title: Routers: The Path Data Takes
chunks.heading: Visual model: hop by hop
chunks.text: Step through a packet's journey across a chain of routers to reach its destination. Curious readers: a real tool called traceroute lets you see the actual chain of routers a packet passes through to reach a given address. You don't need it to understand this module — it's just proof that this "hop by hop" idea is exactly how it really works, not a simplification invented for this page.

chunks.title: What Is a Network?
chunks.text: A network is nothing more mysterious than two or more devices that can send messages to each other. Your phone talking to your laptop over Wi-Fi is a network. Your whole house — phone, laptop, smart TV, all sharing one Wi-Fi router — is a network. And the internet is the same idea, just enormous: it's what you get when huge numbers of separately-run networks all agree to pass each other's messages along.

chunks.title: What Is a Network?
chunks.heading: The internet isn't one thing — it's an agreement
chunks.text: Nobody owns "the internet." Your internet provider runs its own network. A university runs its own network. A company running a big website runs its own network too. What makes it all "the internet" is that these networks agree on common rules for passing messages to each other, so a message from your phone can hop across several different companies' equipment and still arrive at the right place, on the other side of the world, correctly. That's genuinely the whole idea — everything else in this module is detail on how that handoff actually happens.

chunks.title: What Is a Network?
chunks.heading: Most of what you do online is "ask, then answer"
chunks.text: Almost everything you do on a network follows the same shape: your device (the client) asks a question, and some other computer that's always on and waiting (the server) answers it. Loading a web page, opening an app, watching a video — all of it is a client asking a server for something. You've actually already met this exact pattern. In the Databases submodule, Postgres runs as its own server that a client application connects to. It's the same client-server relationship — the only difference here is that the "connection" is happening across a network instead of on one machine.

chunks.title: Files & the File System
chunks.text: A disk, underneath, doesn't actually know what a "file" is. It's just a huge stretch of storage, divided into small fixed-size chunks called blocks. Names, folders, and the neat idea of a "file" are something the operating system builds on top — that layer is called the file system.

chunks.title: Files & the File System
chunks.heading: A file is really just an index entry
chunks.text: When you save a file, its data usually doesn't land in one single tidy chunk of disk — it gets scattered across whichever blocks happen to be free at the time, sometimes not even next to each other. What makes it feel like one coherent "file" is that the file system keeps its own index: a record of exactly which blocks belong to which file, and in what order. Ask for the file by name, and the file system looks it up in that index and reassembles the right blocks for you, instantly. Notice the pattern: this is the same trick you've now seen several times in this section — DNS mapping a name to an address, a packet's pieces reassembled by sequence number, virtual memory mapping a private address to a real one, and now a filename mapping to scattered disk blocks.

chunks.title: Files & the File System
chunks.heading: A file is really just an index entry
chunks.text: Keeping a small lookup table that translates a convenient name into where something really lives shows up everywhere in computing.

chunks.title: Files & the File System
chunks.heading: Where SQLite and Postgres actually live
chunks.text: This is exactly the layer SQLite and Postgres sit on top of. SQLite is famously "just a file" — its entire database really is one file, managed through this exact file-system machinery. Postgres keeps a whole directory of files (its "data directory"), each one holding pages of table and index data, also just ordinary files as far as the file system is concerned. Neither database needs to know or care which physical disk blocks its data ends up in — that's the file system's job, same as it is for a photo or a text file.

chunks.text: Pick a file and see which raw disk blocks it's actually scattered across.

chunks.title: Operating Systems Basics
chunks.text: Your computer is running dozens of programs "at once" — a browser, a chat app, a music player, maybe a database server — on a machine with far fewer CPU cores than that. Something has to decide who gets the CPU, give each program its own private slice of memory, and organize the disk so files don't collide. That referee is the operating system, and this module explains how it does its job, in plain language. This module closes the loop on the whole Computer Functions section: it's the OS that actually hands out the CPU, cache, RAM, disk, and network from the earlier two modules to every program that asks. Grounded, like the rest of this section, in Brendan Gregg's Systems Performance and PlanetScale's engineering blog by Ben Dicken — this time his post on how Postgres and MySQL each handle connections.

chunks.title: Opening an App, Start to Finish
chunks.text: You double-click an icon. A moment later, a window appears, ready to use. Here's everything from this module — and quietly, from the whole Computer Functions section — happening in that short moment.

chunks.title: Opening an App, Start to Finish
chunks.heading: The six steps
chunks.text: Find it — the OS looks up the app's files on disk, using the file system's index. New process — the OS creates a new process for it, with its own private, virtual slice of memory. Load in — the app's actual code is read from disk into that process's memory. Get a turn — the scheduler adds the new process to the rotation and eventually gives it a turn on the CPU. Run — the CPU executes its instructions, leaning on cache and RAM exactly as you saw in the first module. On screen — output reaches the display, and the app is open and responsive.

chunks.title: Opening an App, Start to Finish
chunks.heading: Visual model: watch it happen
chunks.text: Step through it, or hit Auto Play to watch the whole sequence run on its own. This is the payoff of the entire Computer Functions section. Opening an app touches nearly everything you've learned across all three modules: a CPU running instructions with cache and RAM close by, disk storing everything permanently through a file system, a network carrying data between machines when needed, and now an operating system tying all of it together — deciding who gets the CPU, handing out private memory, and organizing the disk. None of these ideas work in isolation; every real program you use leans on all of them, every time.

chunks.title: Processes & Threads
chunks.text: When you open a program, the operating system creates a process for it — a running instance of that program, with its own private slice of memory that nothing else can see or touch. Open the same program twice, and you get two separate processes, each with its own copy of that private memory.

chunks.title: Processes & Threads
chunks.heading: Threads: lighter workers inside one process
chunks.text: A process can also split its own work across multiple threads. Threads live inside one process and share all of that process's memory — unlike two separate processes, which are kept fully apart. Because threads share memory instead of each needing their own private copy, they're much cheaper to create and to switch between. How much cheaper? Switching the CPU from one process to another takes roughly 5 microseconds. Switching between threads takes roughly 1 microsecond — about five times faster — because there's far less bookkeeping involved when everyone's already sharing the same memory.

chunks.title: Processes & Threads
chunks.heading: Two real databases, two different choices
chunks.text: This isn't just theory — it's exactly why Postgres and MySQL are built differently underneath: Postgres uses one process per connection. Every time an application connects, Postgres spawns a whole new OS process to handle it. MySQL runs as a single process ( mysqld) and instead gives each connection its own lightweight thread inside that one process. Processes are safer and more isolated — one connection crashing is less likely to take down another — but heavier, with real memory and CPU overhead per connection. Threads are cheaper and faster to spin up, but share more risk if something goes wrong.

chunks.title: Processes & Threads
chunks.heading: Two real databases, two different choices
chunks.text: Both approaches start to strain once connection counts climb into the thousands, which is exactly why connection poolers exist: a pooler sits between many client connections and the database, and funnels them through a small, fixed set of real connections — typically just 5 to 50 — reusing them instead of creating a new process or thread for every single client.

chunks.title: Scheduling: Taking Turns on the CPU
chunks.text: Recall from the CPU submodule: a single CPU core can only truly run one instruction stream at a time. So how does your computer run dozens of programs "at once" on a handful of cores? It doesn't, really — it just switches between them so quickly that it feels simultaneous. That's the scheduler's job.

chunks.title: Scheduling: Taking Turns on the CPU
chunks.heading: Fast enough turns feel like "at once"
chunks.text: The scheduler gives each runnable process a short slice of CPU time — often just a few milliseconds — then pauses it and lets the next one run. Round and round, dozens of times a second. No single program ever notices the gaps, because each pause is far too short for a human (or even most software) to perceive. That's the whole trick behind multitasking: not true simultaneity, just extremely fast turn-taking.

chunks.title: Scheduling: Taking Turns on the CPU
chunks.heading: Switching isn't free
chunks.text: Every time the scheduler swaps one process out for another, it has to save exactly where that process was and restore the next one's state — a context switch. As you saw in the last submodule, that costs real time: roughly 5 microseconds for a full process switch, about 1 microsecond for a thread. It's tiny compared to a human blink — but if it happens constantly, on a heavily loaded server handling thousands of things at once, those microseconds genuinely add up, which is part of why database designers care so much about how many processes or threads they're juggling.

chunks.title: Virtual Memory
chunks.text: Open your task manager and you might see ten programs, each seemingly convinced it can use huge amounts of memory, starting from address zero, as if it were the only thing running. That's not a coincidence — it's a deliberate illusion the operating system maintains, called virtual memory.

chunks.title: Virtual Memory
chunks.heading: Everyone gets their own private illusion
chunks.text: Every process is handed its own private range of memory addresses to use, called its virtual address space. When that process asks for "address 0x40," the OS (with help from the CPU) quietly translates that into wherever the data actually lives in the computer's real, physical RAM — a location the process never sees or needs to know about. Two completely different programs can both use "address 0x40" and never collide, because underneath, they're mapped to two totally different real locations.

chunks.title: Virtual Memory
chunks.heading: Why bother with the illusion?
chunks.text: Safety — one program can't accidentally (or maliciously) read or overwrite another's memory, because it can't even address it. Simplicity — every program gets to assume it has a clean, private, generously-sized memory space, without needing to coordinate with every other running program about who owns what. Flexibility — the OS is free to physically move a process's data around in real RAM, or even temporarily shuffle rarely-used parts out to disk, without the program ever noticing — the mapping is simply updated underneath it.

chunks.title: Virtual Memory
chunks.heading: Visual model: same address, different reality
chunks.text: Click each program to see what address it believes it's using — and where that's really mapped in physical RAM. This is the same "keep it small and give out only what's currently needed" spirit you saw with RAM's limited capacity in the RAM submodule — virtual memory is the mechanism that lets the OS enforce that fairly and safely across many programs at once.

chunks.title: What Is an Operating System?
chunks.text: Right now, your computer is probably running a browser, a chat app, some background updater, maybe music — all "at once," on a chip with maybe 8 CPU cores. None of those programs know about each other. None of them wrote code to politely take turns or divide up memory fairly. Something else is doing that job for them: the operating system (Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS).

chunks.title: What Is an Operating System?
chunks.heading: A referee with special privileges
chunks.text: The operating system is itself a program — but a special one, with privileges no ordinary app gets. It's the only thing allowed to talk to the hardware directly. Every other program has to ask it for what it needs: "give me some memory," "let me read this file," "send this over the network." The OS decides who gets what, and when — which is exactly what keeps a browser tab from accidentally overwriting your music player's memory, or hogging every last bit of the CPU.

chunks.title: What Is an Operating System?
chunks.heading: What it's actually managing
chunks.text: Everything in this module is really the OS managing the same four things from the earlier modules, just now shared across many programs instead of one: The CPU — who gets to run right now, and for how long (this module's Scheduling submodule). RAM — how it's divided up, and how each program is kept from seeing another's data (Virtual Memory). Disk — how raw storage becomes organized, named files (Files & the File System). The network — which program's request a reply belongs to, and where it should be delivered.
